'''''BioShock 2: Minerva's Den''''' is a [[downloadable content]] (DLC) campaign for the 2010 [[first-person shooter]] game ''[[BioShock 2]]'', developed by [[2K Marin]] and published by [[2K (company)|2K]]. The [[single player]] assumes the role of Subject Sigma, an armored and genetically modified human, or "[[Big Daddy (BioShock)|Big Daddy]]"; Sigma must travel through Minerva's Den, the technological hub of the underwater city of Rapture, to download a schematic of the city's supercomputer. Gameplay is similar to that of ''BioShock 2'', with new enemies and weapons.

''Minerva's Den'' was created by a small team within 2K Marin led by Steve Gaynor, who partly based the setting on ideas he discussed in his hiring interview. The team decided upon a small, personal story about [[Personal identity|identity]] and [[free will]], which explores a previously unseen part of the underwater city of Rapture. ''Minerva's Den'' was initially released for [[PlayStation 3]] and [[Xbox 360]] consoles in August 2010, and was later released and reissued on other platforms. It was well received by critics, who praised its story, characters, and gameplay; reviewers, including those writing for ''[[Kotaku]]'' and ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'', considered it one of the best video game expansions of all time. The experience of creating a small, story-focused project inspired Gaynor and other 2K employees to form [[Fullbright (company)|The Fullbright Company]] and create ''[[Gone Home]]'' (2013).

== Gameplay ==
{{see also|BioShock 2#Gameplay}}
Like ''[[BioShock 2]]'', ''Minerva's Den'' is a [[first-person shooter]] game. The story takes place in the underwater city of [[Rapture (BioShock)|Rapture]] in 1968,<ref name="venturebeat-bioshock 2 interview" /> eight years after the events of ''[[BioShock]]'' and concurrent with the events of ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2''{{'}}s story mode, in the technological district of Minerva's Den.<ref name="pcgamesn-minerva's den review" /> The player character, Subject Sigma, is a [[Big Daddy (BioShock)|Big Daddy]], a person fused with an armored [[diving suit]].<ref name="venturebeat-bioshock 2 interview" /> The player must work with the scientist Charles Milton Porter to acquire the plans of his creation, a [[supercomputer]] known as the Thinker, and escape Rapture.<ref name="ign-minerva's den review" /> Opposing the player are enemies known as splicers—Rapture's residents who overused genetic modifications<ref name="1up-bioshock review" />—along with other Big Daddies and automated security.<ref name="ign-minerva's den review" /> The game can be completed in between three and five hours.<ref name="rollingstone-minerva's den walking sim" /><ref name="games radar-minerva's den review" />

The gameplay of ''Minerva's Den'' is similar to that of ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2''. The player uses similar weapons and plasmids (genetic modifications that grant superpowers)<ref name="arstechnica-plasmids">{{cite web|author=Westgarth, Michael|date=February 12, 2014|url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2014/02/science-is-slowly-building-towards-real-life-bioshock-like-plasmids/|title=Science inches closer to real BioShock-style plasmids|website=[[Ars Technica]]|publisher=Condé Nast|access-date=January 4, 2020|archive-date=January 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109223935/https://arstechnica.com/science/2014/02/science-is-slowly-building-towards-real-life-bioshock-like-plasmids/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="gamesradar-plasmidguide">{{cite web|author=Barratt, Charlie|date=August 17, 2007|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/bioshock-plasmid-guide/|title=BioShock Plasmid Guide|website=[[GamesRadar+]]|publisher=Future Publishing|access-date=January 3, 2020|archive-date=January 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200103200535/https://www.gamesradar.com/bioshock-plasmid-guide/|url-status=live}}</ref> but obtains them in a different order,<ref name="ign-minerva's den review" /> with an increased emphasis on hacking security.<ref name="ign-minerva's den review" /> The expansion adds new items, including the Ion Lance, a laser weapon wielded by Minerva's Den's Lancer Big Daddies,<ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" /> and the Gravity Well plasmid, which stuns and pulls enemies towards a vortex. New enemies include security robots armed with rockets or laser weapons, flame-wielding Brute Splicers, and ice-throwing Houdini Splicers.<ref name="ign-minerva's den review" /><ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" /><ref name="ign-minerva's den preview" />

== Plot ==
Subject Sigma is guided by the voice of Charles Milton Porter as he approaches Minerva's Den, Rapture's central computer core. Porter wants to reach his supercomputer, the Thinker, to retrieve its blueprints so he can recreate it on the surface.<ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" /> Sigma is opposed by Porter's former colleague Reed Wahl,<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock" /> whom Porter warns has become insane from splicing and his obsession with the Thinker.<ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" />

After becoming disillusioned with his role in [[World War II]] and the loss of his wife Pearl in [[The Blitz]], Porter traveled to Rapture to pursue his dreams of creating [[artificial intelligence]].<ref name="2k-minerva's den bts 2" /> While initially working together, Porter and Wahl each wanted to use the Thinker for their own ends. Porter attempted to recreate Pearl by emulating her personality with the Thinker, while Wahl believed he could program the computer to predict the future.<ref name="eurogamer-minerva's den retrospective" /> Wahl betrayed Porter to Rapture's secret police to keep the Thinker for himself.<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock" /> Minerva's Den has been cut off from the rest of Rapture, and its scientists, who have taken to splicing, attack Sigma.<ref name="minerva's den-porter1quote" />

As Sigma progresses, the environment becomes increasingly threatening due to the Thinker's sophisticated defense system and interference from Wahl and his forces. Sigma reaches the Thinker's core where he confronts and kills Wahl.<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock" /> Sampling Sigma's DNA to print out its schematics, the Thinker reveals Sigma's true identity as Porter, who was turned into a Big Daddy after being handed over to Rapture's authorities.<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock" /> Porter's "instructions" throughout the game actually came from the Thinker, imitating the voice of one of its creators.<ref name="minerva's den-tenenbaum1quote" /> The final sequence of the game contains no combat; the player walks through Porter's living quarters, where he obsessed over digitally recreating his wife.<ref name="eurogamer-minerva's den retrospective" /> Sigma and the scientist [[Brigid Tenenbaum]] return to the surface in a [[bathysphere]]; Tenenbaum is able to undo Sigma's programming and restore Porter's original human body. Porter visits his wife's grave and leaves a letter in which he apologizes for trying to bring her back using the Thinker, and says he has decided to let her go.<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock" />

== Development ==
[[File:The Fullbright Company - Game Developers Choice Awards 2014.jpg|thumb|right|Steve Gaynor (second from left), Johnnemann Nordhagen (third) and Karla Zimonja (fourth) were members of the team that developed ''Minerva's Den''.|alt=Four smiling people (two women and two men) stand in front of a podium. Behind them is a large blue screen with the words THE FULLBRIGHT COMPANY projected across it.]]

Development of the ''Minerva's Den'' [[downloadable content]] (DLC) began after the completion of ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2''. Steve Gaynor and a team of nine other full-time workers were tasked with creating a three-to-five-hour, single-player experience;<ref name="2K-minerva's den easter eggs" /> Gaynor served as lead designer and writer, having worked as a level designer for ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' and on story elements such as dialogue and audio diaries—scattered logs that reveal backstory while players explore,<ref name="gamasutra-building bioshock 2" /><ref name="rockpapershotgun-audio logs"/> Devin St. Clair as lead artist and Jeff Fisher as lead programmer.<ref name="2K-minerva's den easter eggs" /> The names of the development team were given to slugs scattered around the game's levels as an [[Easter egg (software)|Easter egg]].<ref name="2K-minerva's den easter eggs" /> The development team were limited in what form the DLC could take and had to reuse as many assets as possible; Gaynor recalled the constraints of limited time and resources was a blessing in disguise.<ref name="inverse-gaynor interview" /> Though many companies would treat DLC as a "cash grab" with less development time and lowered expectations, Gaynor felt these constraints also enabled more creative risks to be taken.<ref name="rollingstone-minerva's den walking sim" /> With such a small team, the staff collaborated without remaining in segregated roles; according to Gaynor, "It has to be organic as possible, and when someone has something that's not necessarily their primary responsibility but they have a passion for it and ideas for it&nbsp;... I think you have to take advantage of that".<ref name="gamasutra-building bioshock 2" />

While being interviewed for his job at 2K Marin, Gaynor had been asked to propose a potential ''BioShock'' level. Gaynor recalled suggesting a story focusing on Rapture's computer core and a character splicing to become more intelligent. During ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2''{{'}}s development, the level designers suggested the possibility that technology from Rapture created a primitive artificial intelligence (A.I.) that would lead to the development of [[SHODAN]], an A.I. that appears in the video game ''[[System Shock]]''. When developing ideas for what would become ''Minerva's Den'', Gaynor suggested merging the ideas, using a story about Rapture's computer core and a "[[steampunk]]" A.I., drawing from SHODAN's multiple identities and impersonations.<ref name="bleedingcool-system shock link" /> Gaynor wanted the content to fit both the world of ''BioShock'' and the historical era in which it takes place. When the developers decided to focus on Rapture's computer technology, they based it on the [[History of computing hardware#Advent of the digital computer|early computing age]] spurred by work done during World War II, including the work of [[Alan Turing]] and the cryptographers at [[Bletchley Park]].<ref name="2k-minerva's den bts 1" /> Gaynor reasoned that Rapture advanced using genetic technology, but the residents of Rapture explored other technological dead ends, including areas devoted to robotics and automation in Minerva's Den.<ref name="gamasutra-building bioshock 2" />

Contrasting the long development and narrative of the main game with those of Minerva's Den, Gaynor said that he enjoyed the opportunity to tell a shorter story where players understood the characters.<ref name="portlandmercury-goinghome" /> According to Gaynor:
<blockquote>We could take the themes of ''BioShock'' that are native to Rapture and make them relevant to the specific fiction of ''Minerva's Den''. When you have a super computer that can do a million calculations a second, how does that fit into the [[BioShock (series)#Themes|ideas of free will and predestination and fate, and choice]], that ''BioShock'' is built on?<ref name="eurogamer-minerva's den retrospective" /></blockquote>

Gaynor wanted to adapt the grand themes of ''BioShock'' to tell a different story about loss and changing the past that focused on a single character, Porter, who forms the "heart" of the game.<ref name="eurogamer-minerva's den retrospective" /><ref name="gamasutra-gone home" /> Gaynor felt the final gameplay sequence, in which the player walks through Porter's living space, was important to give players time to reflect on the character's journey.<ref name="eurogamer-minerva's den retrospective" /> He resisted calls to make the interesting environment a place for combat.<ref name="rollingstone-minerva's den walking sim" />

To prevent players of ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' from feeling ''Minerva's Den''{{'}}s gameplay was repetitive, 2K Marin tried to present a different experience within the narrative's constraints. Shadowy level design and more dangerous enemies were crafted to give a subtle [[survival horror]] feel; the team also adjusted the order in which players receive equipment and plasmids to encourage them to interact with the environment, rather than simply using aggression.<ref name="gamasutra-building bioshock 2" />

== Release ==
''Minerva's Den'' was announced as the final piece of ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' DLC in August 2010.<ref name="wired-minerva's den announce" /> ''Minerva's Den'' is the only expansion for the game to offer new single-player experiences.<ref name="gamespot-minerva's den announce" /> The DLC was released on August 31 for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 consoles,<ref name="joystiq-minerva's den release" /> with minimal promotion.<ref name="gamasutra-building bioshock 2" /> Initially, there were no plans to release ''Minerva's Den'' and other ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' DLC for [[personal computer]]s (PCs)<ref name="gameinformer-minerva's den never PC" /><ref name="kotaku-minerva's den never PC" /> but 2K later resumed development of the PC ports, and ''Minerva's Den'' was released for [[Microsoft Windows]] in 2011 and for [[macOS|OS X]] in 2015.<ref name="engadget-minerva's den pc release" /><ref name="gamereactor-minerva's den mac" />

With the closure of the [[Games for Windows]] Live Marketplace in August 2013, ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' and all of its DLC was released on [[Steam (service)|Steam]] in October 2013. The game was updated to support Steam [[Achievement (video games)|achievements]], [[Steam (service)#User interface|Big Picture mode]], and [[gamepad|controllers]]. ''Minerva's Den'' was free for players who owned ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' before the update.<ref name="ign-bioshock 2 games for windows closing" /><ref name="destructoid-bioshock 2 steam" /><ref name="polygon-bioshock 2 steam" /> In January 2013, ''Minerva's Den'' and the rest of ''BioShock 2'' were rereleased in a bundle with ''BioShock'' as ''BioShock: Ultimate Rapture Edition''.<ref name="eurogamer-ultimate rapture edition" /> ''Minerva's Den'' was also included in the remastered 2016 ''BioShock'' compilation ''[[BioShock: The Collection]]'', which has been released for Windows, [[PlayStation 4]], [[Xbox One]] and [[Nintendo Switch]].<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock" /><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/nintendo/2020/3/26/21195331/nintendo-switch-direct-mini-release-date-announcements-bioshock-borderlands | title = BioShock, Borderlands games coming to Nintendo Switch in May | first = Nicole | last = Carpenter | date = March 26, 2020 | access-date = March 26, 2020 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = November 21, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201121120249/https://www.polygon.com/nintendo/2020/3/26/21195331/nintendo-switch-direct-mini-release-date-announcements-bioshock-borderlands | url-status = live }}</ref>

== Reception and legacy ==
{{Video game reviews
| MC = PS3: 81/100<ref name="MC_PS3" /><br />X360: 82/100<ref name="MC_X360" />
|PCGUS=81/100<ref name="pcgamer-minerva's den review" />
|GI=85/100<ref name="gameinformer-minerva's den review" />
|GSpot=8.5/10<ref name="gamespot-minerva's den review" />
|GRadar=9/10<ref name="games radar-minerva's den review" />

}}
''Minerva's Den'' received generally favorable reviews, according to review aggregator [[Metacritic]].<ref name="MC_X360" /> ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' praised ''Minerva's Den'' after the lackluster ''BioShock 2'' DLC that preceded it,<ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" /> and ''[[Eurogamer]]'' and ''[[IGN]]'' called it an excellent finale story for the setting of Rapture.<ref name="ign-minerva's den review" /><ref name="eurogamer-ultimate rapture edition"/> ''Minerva's Den'' has been called one of the greatest DLC expansions of all time.<ref name="pcgamesn-minerva's den review" /><ref name="kotaku-best expansions" /><ref name="paste-dlc" /><ref name="gamerant-dlc" />

Critics said ''Minerva's Den'' plays much the same as ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2''<ref name="pcgamesn-minerva's den review" /><ref name="games radar-minerva's den review" /><ref name="rockpapershotgun-minerva's den review_j70ng"/> but welcomed the new additions to gameplay.<ref name="gameinformer-minerva's den review" /> Several reviewers felt the expansion offered a complete, concentrated ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' experience;<ref name="gamespot-minerva's den review" /><ref name="engadget-minerva's den review" /> ''[[Rock, Paper, Shotgun]]'' wrote ''Minerva's Den'' "hits the key beats of the ideas behind ''BioShock''—manipulation, twisted technology, distorted values, ambition and folly—and it weaves all that into the improved combat system that, for some, makes ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2'' the superior of ''BioShock 1''".<ref name="rockpapershotgun-minerva's den review_j70ng" /> ''Kotaku'' and ''[[Engadget]]'' found aspects of the gameplay repetitive, such as the reuse of "tedious" elements from the base game, and the need to perform certain gameplay sequences repeatedly.<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den review" /><ref name="engadget-minerva's den review" />

Reviewers praised the narrative of ''Minerva's Den.''<ref name="ign-minerva's den review" /><ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" /><ref name="gameinformer-minerva's den review" /> ''[[GamesRadar+|GamesRadar]]''{{'}}s Andrew Heyward said the story makes ''Minerva's Den'' a "must-play extension" of the game's universe,<ref name="games radar-minerva's den review" /> and ''GameSpot''{{'}}s Kevin VanOrd wrote that while the setup for the expansion is familiar to ''BioShock'' players—voices on the radio telling the player where to go—the appeal lies with its "personal nature" and Porter's character.<ref name="gamespot-minerva's den review" /> Reviews from ''GameSpot'' and ''Eurogamer'' considered Wahl a weak villain, but Porter a compelling protagonist.<ref name="eurogamer-minerva's den retrospective" /><ref name="gamespot-minerva's den review" /> The [[video game theorist]] Robert Gallagher praised the game as a thoughtful and complex examination of themes of technology and humanity, and evidence that video games could explore such topics well.<ref name="gallagher-video games"/>

The game's twist ending was positively received;<ref name="pcgamesn-minerva's den review" /><ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" /><ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock"/> VanOrd called it "surprising from a plot perspective and thematically consistent with prior ''BioShock'' revelations"<ref name="gamespot-minerva's den review" /> though ''Engadget'' said that while the twist applies a retroactive motivation for the characters, it comes at the expense of the player's link to Subject Sigma.<ref name="engadget-minerva's den review" /> ''Kotaku''{{'}}s Heather Alexandra contrasted the twist with those of ''BioShock'' and ''[[BioShock Infinite]]'', writing, "[those] games want to impress you. ''Minerva's Den'' wants to move you."<ref name="kotaku-minerva's den best bioshock" /> Several reviewers felt the expansion's story stronger than that of ''BioShock{{nbsp}}2''.<ref name="games radar-minerva's den review" /><ref name="dailytelegraph-minerva's den review" />

Gaynor credited the positive experience with a small development team for changing his perception of creating games.<ref name="portlandmercury-goinghome" /> Gaynor later joined [[Irrational Games]], and his resulting dissatisfaction with the sprawling development of ''BioShock Infinite'' led Gaynor and two other ''Minerva's Den'' developers to start their own game studio, [[Fullbright (company)|The Fullbright Company]].<ref name="portlandmercury-goinghome" /><ref name="bleedingcool-gaynor fullbright" /> Fullbright developed the acclaimed game ''[[Gone Home]]'', which shares ''Minerva's Den''{{'}}s nonlinear exploration and character focus.<ref name="rollingstone-minerva's den walking sim" /><ref name="pcgamer-gone home interview" /> The final non-combat exploration sequence of ''Minerva's Den'' served as a template for ''Gone Home''.<ref name="rollingstone-minerva's den walking sim" />
